The storm had been beating against the base of the lighthouse for three days when Eamon found the bottle.

He'd gone down to the storage cellar for more kerosene—old habits, even though the lamp had been automated a decade ago and the tower belonged now to some coastal authority in Dublin that sent checks and sent no one else. His boots left wet prints on the stone floor as he hauled the last tin from its shelf, and that was when he saw it, wedged beneath a coil of rope and a stack of water-stained manifests. Green glass, wax-sealed, the cork dark with years of salt water.

He carried it up to the keeper's quarters, set it on the narrow table beside the window, and stared at it for a long time. The glass was frosted with dried brine. The label, a scrap of oilcloth, bore a single word in ink so faded it was almost gone
